title: Household DNS filtering
body_md:
## DNS answers a name before a connection

When a device opens a site, it commonly asks a DNS resolver where that domain points. A filtering resolver may refuse names it classifies as malware or phishing. Cloudflare's **plain** 1.1.1.1 is a general resolver, not the same as its Families malware-filtering addresses 1.1.1.2/1.0.0.2. Families returns a blocking address for a classified domain. Other providers use different lists, categories, test pages and privacy policies. Select a provider only after reading its scope and data handling. DNS filtering can stop a known malicious domain before a page loads, but it cannot judge a seller's intent, inspect encrypted page content or reliably classify every new lookalike. A legitimate domain can be mistakenly blocked.

## Decide where the policy should apply

Configuring a router can cover devices that use its DNS settings while at home; configuring one device is narrower and easier to test. A local DNS blocker such as Pi-hole adds control but needs a maintained host and may expose query logs to its administrator. The scope depends on the setting: a DNS choice saved only for one Wi-Fi network need not apply on cellular, while Android system-wide Private DNS can use the chosen resolver on both Wi-Fi and cellular. Browser secure DNS, a VPN or an app can also choose a different resolver. Thus “set on the router” does not mean “protects every device everywhere.” Encrypted DNS protects queries on the path to the chosen resolver; it does not automatically filter or validate websites. If another person manages the home network, agree on policy and a way to reverse it before changing shared settings.

## Test, investigate, reverse

Write down the original DNS setting before changing it. Use the resolver's documented safe test page or domain; do not test by visiting a live malicious site. Check a device on home Wi-Fi and, separately, cellular or another network if relevant. If a needed site fails, check whether the chosen resolver blocked it rather than assuming the site is dangerous. Confirm the service's true address through an independent channel. Cloudflare Families documents anonymous feedback for a mistaken classification, but its fixed modes provide no documented per-domain allow control or household query log. A report does not promise an immediate unblock. If only one device's Wi-Fi DNS was changed and access is urgent, deliberately restore its recorded trusted DNS setting for the confirmed task, then restore and retest Families. While switched, Families no longer filters lookups using that Wi-Fi DNS setting. If the resolver is unavailable, restore your recorded settings or use a trusted fallback. DNS is a layer beneath browser warnings, updates, MFA and independent verification; a successful DNS lookup is never a safety verdict.

widget_config.goal: Set one household DNS filter deliberately, test its scope, and recover from a false block without abandoning safer browsing habits.
widget_config.today_action: Identify the current resolver and setting type on one device. If you test a filter, use a provider-documented safe test domain on Wi-Fi and cellular, and note whether the setting is Wi-Fi-only, system-wide Private DNS or overridden by the browser.
widget_config.scope: Home-network explanation checked 2026-10-20. Cloudflare addresses are one provider example, not a universal recommendation; device menus and Wi-Fi-only versus system-wide settings vary. Families has fixed modes and a miscategorization-feedback path, not a documented per-domain allow control. Categories can be wrong or lag behind new sites.

blocks.title: A new fake benefits from the gap
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a family member receives a parcel notice naming a newly created parcel-themed domain. In this invented case the domain resolves, but the filter has not classified it; no real link is supplied.
blocks.analysis: A DNS answer in this scenario means only that this resolver did not block the lookup. The family opens the retailer’s order history through a saved app and does not enter credentials at the message address. No real domain is offered for testing.

blocks.title: School portal blocked by category
blocks.situation: Synthetic: after Cloudflare Families malware filtering is enabled for one test phone's Wi-Fi profile, a known school portal stops loading; the school independently confirms its official domain.
blocks.analysis: This may be a false positive. The family checks the phone's DNS setting and submits Cloudflare's anonymous miscategorization feedback. Families has no documented per-domain allow or household query log; feedback does not promise immediate access. For an urgent school task, they may temporarily restore this phone's recorded trusted DNS, visit the independently confirmed portal, then restore and retest Families. That temporary switch removes Families filtering for lookups using this phone's Wi-Fi DNS setting.

blocks.title: Pilot a home DNS policy
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise: four independent test-device checkpoints. Each prompt states the active DNS setup; no shared router is changed and no live risky domain is opened.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 1: a test device supports DNS settings for one Wi-Fi network. You want malware filtering and see 1.1.1.1 and 1.1.1.2. What do you choose?

choices.text: Set the documented Families malware-filtering resolver in this test Wi-Fi profile.
choices.consequence: This Wi-Fi profile uses a resolver with the requested category; other networks are not configured by this step.
choices.explanation: Plain 1.1.1.1 is not the Families filter.

choices.text: Use plain 1.1.1.1 and assume it blocks malware.
choices.explanation: Resolver names and policies must be checked, not guessed.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 2: on a separate test device, Families is selected in settings. How will you verify filtering without browsing a real scam?

choices.text: Search for a current malware link and open it.
choices.explanation: Never require a live malicious destination for a lesson or setup test.

choices.text: Use the provider’s documented safe test domain and record the result.
choices.consequence: You test the setup without exposure to a malicious page.
choices.explanation: Provider test endpoints are built for this purpose.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 3: Families is configured only for a test phone’s home Wi-Fi, not as system-wide Private DNS. The safe provider test blocks on Wi-Fi but not cellular. What does that show?

choices.text: The shared router must be broken.
choices.consequence: You may change a working setup for the wrong reason.
choices.explanation: No router setting changed here, and the phone can use different DNS across network types.

choices.text: The Wi-Fi-only DNS choice did not follow the phone to cellular; document that boundary.
choices.consequence: You distinguish this Wi-Fi profile from the phone’s cellular DNS behavior.
choices.explanation: This result fits a per-Wi-Fi setting; Android system-wide Private DNS can apply on cellular too.

steps.prompt: Checkpoint 4: on another test phone with Families configured only for its Wi-Fi profile, an independently confirmed school portal is blocked. What next?

choices.text: Confirm the phone's DNS setting and report the possible false positive to Cloudflare. For urgent access, temporarily restore this phone's recorded trusted DNS, then reinstate Families.
choices.consequence: Feedback is submitted. A temporary device-level switch may enable access, but Families filtering is absent for lookups using that phone's Wi-Fi DNS setting until restored; no instant provider unblock is promised.
choices.explanation: Families documents feedback for miscategorization, not a per-domain allow rule. Confirm the portal through a known school channel first.

choices.text: Turn off all protection and never revisit it.
choices.consequence: The phone loses its filtering indefinitely because of one block.
choices.explanation: Reporting the possible error and a deliberate, reversible change on one device are available without assuming an instant provider fix.

blocks.debrief: Replay by separating resolver choice, per-Wi-Fi versus system-wide scope, provider test result and the separate question whether a site is trustworthy.

questions.prompt: What does plain Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 do in this lesson?

choices.text: Resolves names without the Families malware category.
choices.explanation: The filtering service has distinct addresses.

choices.text: Guarantees that every phishing domain is blocked.
choices.explanation: Neither plain DNS nor a filter can guarantee that.

questions.prompt: A filtered domain resolves successfully. What can you infer?

choices.explanation: DNS does not authenticate a seller.

choices.text: Only that this resolver did not block this lookup.
choices.explanation: A new or misclassified scam site can pass.

questions.prompt: Why may a browser ignore your router’s DNS filter?

choices.text: Its secure-DNS setting may use another resolver.
choices.explanation: Some browser configurations choose their own path.

choices.text: Router DNS always controls all browser queries.
choices.explanation: That ignores secure DNS and other overrides.

questions.prompt: A known service is blocked. Best first step?

choices.text: Assume it is criminal and warn everyone.
Independently confirm its domain and inspect the block reason.
choices.explanation: It could be a true or false positive.
